## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.91243.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.91243.3.sa2)

This manuscript examines how humans walk over uneven terrain and use vision to decide where to step. There is a huge lack of evidence about this because the vast majority of locomotion studies have focused on steady, well-controlled conditions, and not on decisions made in the real world. The author team has already made great advances in this topic by pioneering gaze recordings during locomotion, but there has been no practical way to map the gaze targets, specifically the 3D terrain features in naturalistic environments. The team has now developed a way to integrate such measurements along with gaze and step tracking. This allows quantitative evaluation of the proposed trade-offs between stepping vertically onto vs. stepping around obstacles, along with how far people look to decide where to step. The team also introduces several new analysis techniques to accompany these measurements. They use machine learning techniques to examine whether retinocentric depth helps predict footholds and develop simulations to assess possible alternative footholds and walking paths. The technical achievement is impressive.

This study addresses several real-world questions not normally examined in the laboratory. First, do humans elect to walk around steeper footholds rather than over them? Second, is there a quantifiable benefit to walking around, such as allowing for a flatter path? Third, does visual depth of terrain contribute to selection of footholds? Fourth, are there scale effects, where for example a tall adult can easily walk over an obstacle that a toddler must walk around. One might superficially answer yes to all of these questions, but it is highly nontrival to answer them quantitatively. As for the conclusions, my feelings are mixed. I find strengths in answers to two of the questions, and weaknesses in the other two.

Strengths:

I consider the evidence strongest for the first of the main questions. The results show subjects walking with more laterally deviating paths, measured by a quantity called "tortuosity," when the direct straight-ahead paths appear to have steeper ups and downs (Fig. 9). The measure of straight-ahead steepness is fairly complicated (discussed below), but is shown to be well correlated with tortuosity, effectively predicting when subjects will not walk straight ahead.

There is also good evidence for the third question, showing that retinocentric depth is predictive of chosen footholds. Retinocentric depth was computed by a series of steps, starting with scene capture to determine a 3D terrain mesh, projecting that mesh into the eye's perspective, and then discarding all but the depth information. This highly involved process is only the beginning, because the depth was then used to train a neural network classifier with chosen footholds. That network was found to predict footholds better than chance, using a test set independent from the training set, each using half the recorded data. The results are strong and are best interpreted along with a previous study (Bonnen et al. 2021) showing that subjects gaze nearer ahead on rougher terrain, and slightly more so when binocular vision was disrupted. Depth information seems important for foothold selection.

As an aside, humans presumably also select footholds and estimate depth from a number of monocular visual cues, such as shading, shadows, color, and self-motion information. Interestingly, the terrain mesh and depth data here were computed from monocular images, suggesting that monocular vision can in principle be predictive of both depth and footholds. Binocular human vision presumably improves on monocular depth estimation, and so it would be interesting to see whether binocular scene cameras would predict footholds better. In an earlier review, I had suggested other avenues for exploration, but these are not weaknesses so much as opportunities not yet taken. I believe much could be learned from deeper analysis of the neural network, and future experiments using variations of this technique.

There is much to be appreciated about this study. I was impressed by the overarching outlook and ambitiousness of the team. They seek to understand human decision-making in real-world locomotion tasks, a topic of obvious relevance to the human condition but not often examined in research. The field has been biased toward well-controlled, laboratory studies, which have undeniable scientific advantages but are also quite different from the real world. The present study discards all of the usual advantages of the laboratory, yet still finds a way to explore real-world behaviors in a quantitative manner. It is an exciting and forward-thinking approach, used to tackle an ecologically relevant question.

I also appreciate the numerous technical challenges of this study. The state of the art in real-world locomotion studies has largely been limited to kinematic motion capture. This team managed to collect and analyze an unprecedented, one-of-a-kind dataset. They applied a number of non-trivial methods to assess retinocentric depth, simulate would-be walking paths and steepness, and predict footholds from neural network. Any of these could and probably will merit individual papers, and to assemble them all at once is quite beyond other studies I am aware of. I hope this study will spur more inquiries of this type, leveraging mobile electronics and modern machine learning techniques to answer questions that were previously only addressable qualitatively.

Weaknesses:

Although I am highly enthusiastic about this study, I was not entirely convinced by the evidence for the second and fourth questions. Some of this is because I was confused by aspects of the analysis, limiting my understanding of the evidence. But I also question some of the basic conclusions, whether the authors indeed proved that (from Abstract, emphasis mine) "[walkers] change direction TO AVOID taking steeper steps that involve large height changes, instead of [sic] choosing more circuitous, RELATIVELY FLAT paths." (I interpret the "of" as a typo that should have been omitted). I think it is more objective to say, "walkers changed direction more when straight-ahead paths seemed to have steeper height changes."

I say "seemed" because it is unknown whether humans would have experienced greater height changes if they walked straight ahead (the second main question). The comparison shown is between human tortuous paths taken and simulated straight-ahead paths never experienced by human. Ignoring questions about the simulations for now (discussed below), it is not an apples-to-apples comparison, say between the tortuous paths humans preferred and straight-ahead paths they didn't. The authors determined a measure of steepness, "straight path slope" (Fig. 9), that predicts when humans circuitously, but that is the same as the steepness that humans would actually experience if they had walked straight ahead. That could have been measured with an appropriate control condition, for example asking subjects to walk as straight ahead as they can manage. That also would have eliminated the need for simulations, because the slope of each step actually taken could simply have been measured and compared between conditions. Instead, two different kinds of simulations are compared, where steeper paths are fully simulated, and the circuitous paths are partially simulated but partially based on data. It seems that every fifth circuitous step coincides with a human foothold, but the intervening ones are somewhat random. I don't find this especially strong evidence that the chosen paths were indeed relatively flatter. I would prefer to be convinced by hard data than by unequal simulations.

I also have trouble accepting "TO AVOID" because it implies a degree of intent not evident in the data. I suppose conscious intent could be assessed subjectively by questionnaire, but I don't know how unconscious intent could be tested objectively. I believe my suggested interpretation above is better supported by evidence.

My limited acceptance is due in part to confusion about the simulations. I was especially confused about the connection between feasible steps drawn from the distribution in Figure 7, and the histograms of Figure 8. The feasible steps have clear peaks near zero slope, unity step length, and zero step direction (let's call them Flat). If 5-step simulations of Figure 8 draw from that distribution, why is there zero probability for the 0-3 deg bin (which is within {plus minus}3 deg due to absolute values)? It seems to me that Flat steps were eminently available, so why were they completely avoided? It seems that the simulations were probabilistic (and not just figurative) random walks, which implies they should have had about the same mean as Figure 7 but a wider variance, and then passed through absolute value. They look like something else that I cannot understand. This is important because the RELATIVELY FLAT conclusion is based on the chosen walks apparently being skewed flatter than random simulated walks. I have trouble accepting those distributions because Flat steps were unaccountably never taken by either simulation or human. (This issue is less concerning for Figure 9, because one can accept that some simulation measure is predictive of tortuosity even if the measure is hard to understand).

I was also confused why Figure 7 distances and directions are nearly normally distributed and not more uniform. The methods only mention constraints to eliminate steps, which to me suggests a truncated uniform distribution. It is not clear to me why the terrain should have a high peak at unity step length, which implies that the only feasible footholds were almost exclusively straight ahead and one step length away. It is possible that the "feasible" footholds are themselves drawn from a "likely" normal distribution, perhaps based on level walking data. It could be argued that simulated steps should be performed by drawing from typical step distributions for level ground, eliminating non-viable footholds, and then repeating that across multiple steps. That would explain the normality, but it is not stated in the Methods, and even if they were "feasible and likely" it would not explain the distributions of Figure 8.

I had some misgivings about the fourth question, where Figure 10 suggests that shorter subjects had greater correlation between straight-path slope and tortuosity than taller ones, who tended to walk straighter ahead. I agree with the authors' rebuttal to my previous review that "the data are the data" but I still have doubts. Now supplied as suggested by another reviewer, Figure 18 provides more detail of the underlying data, with considerably lower correlations. I now suspect that Figure 10 benefits from some statistical artifacts due to binning and other operations, and the weaker correlations of Fig. 18A are closer to reality. I am rather suspicious of correlations of correlations (Figure 18B), which lose some statistical grounding because the second correlation treats all data on equal footing, effectively whitewashing the first correlations of their varying significance (p-values 0.008 to 1e-9).

Furthermore, I am also unsure about Figure 10's comparison of tortuosity vs. straight path slope against leg length. Both tortuosity and straight path slope are already effectively dimensionless and therefore already seem to eliminate scale. It is my understanding that the simulated paths were recomputed for each subject's parameters, and the horizontal axis, slope, is already an angular measure that should affect short and tall people similarly. Shouldn't all subjects equally avoid steep angles, regardless of their dimensional height? If there is indeed a scale effect, then I would expect it to be demonstrated with a dimensional measure (vertical axis) that depends on leg length.

I certainly agree with the hypothetical prior that tall adults walk straight over obstacles that shorter adults (or children) walk around. But I feel that simpler tests would better evidence, perhaps in future work. Did shorter subjects walk with greater tortuosity than taller ones on the same terrain? Did shorter subjects take relatively more steps even after normalizing for leg length? A possible comparison would be (number of steps)*(leg length)/(start to end distance). I feel that the evidence from this study is not that strong.

Although it is a strength of this study that so much can be learned from pure observation, that does not mean controlled conditions are not scientifically helpful. As mentioned earlier, a helpful control could have been to ask subjects to walk straighter but less preferred paths on the same terrain, treating human paths as an independent variable. Another would be to treat terrain as an independent variable, by using level ground and intermediate terrain conditions. This would make it easier to test whether taller subjects walk straighter ahead on more uneven terrain than shorter subjects. Indeed, the data set already includes some patches of flatter terrain, not included here. Additional and simpler tests might be possible based on existing data.

Conclusion

This is an ambitious undertaking, presenting a wealth of unprecedented data to quantitatively test basic ecological questions that have long been unanswered. There are a number of considerable strengths that merit appreciation, especially the ability to quantitatively predict when humans will walk more circuitously. The weaknesses are about limitations in the conclusions that can be drawn thus far rather than the correctness of the study. I consider this to be a first step that will hopefully enable and inspire a long line of future work that will address these questions more in depth.

results.result: The authors developed a photogrammetry-based terrain reconstruction method that achieves median reconstruction errors of 4.5 cm for the overall terrain and 4.0 cm at foothold locations, which is substantially below the average foot length (25.8 cm). This method eliminates parallax errors from flat ground plane assumptions and IMU drift errors present in previous work.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 provide quantitative validation of reconstruction accuracy with appropriate context (C27-C28). The method addresses specific limitations of prior work (C104-C106) and the error magnitudes are reasonable for the application. The validation approach comparing multiple reconstructions of the same terrain is sound.

results.result: A convolutional neural network trained on retinocentric depth images achieved above-chance performance (median AUC > 0.5) in predicting foothold locations for all nine subjects, demonstrating that depth information contributes to foothold selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 show consistent above-chance CNN performance across all subjects using appropriate train-test splits. This finding is consistent with prior work (C29) showing depth information affects gaze patterns. The AUC metric appropriately quantifies discriminability between foothold and non-foothold locations.

results.result: Walkers prefer flatter paths: the median chosen path segment slope (mean 9.5° ± 1.7°) was significantly lower than simulated viable path slopes (mean 14.9° ± 3.3°), with simulated slopes being 5.56° larger on average (t(8)=7.64, p<<0.001). This preference is consistent with minimizing energetic costs associated with vertical displacement.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C43 provide strong quantitative evidence with appropriate statistical testing. The simulation approach constrains viable paths based on biomechanical limits (C35) and individual walking parameters. The interpretation regarding energetic costs (C32-C34) is well-supported by cited literature, though direct energetic measurements were not performed.

results.result: Walkers choose more tortuous (curved) paths to avoid height changes: path tortuosity increased with the slope of straight alternative paths. At the lowest slope levels, average tortuosity was near 1 (straight), but increased across increasing quantiles of straight path slope, indicating a trade-off between path directness and flatness.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C54 provide comprehensive quantitative characterization of the tortuosity-slope relationship. The analysis appropriately compares chosen paths to simulated straight alternatives with fixed endpoints. The observed pattern (C53-C54) supports the interpretation of a trade-off (C55), though the correlation is modest and variable across subjects.

results.result: The strength of the slope-tortuosity trade-off varies with walker biomechanics: longer leg lengths were associated with lower correlation coefficients between straight path slope and tortuosity (r=-0.83, p=0.005), suggesting that walkers with shorter legs are more likely to choose longer paths to avoid steep slopes.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 demonstrate a significant relationship between leg length and path selection strategy with appropriate statistical support. This finding is mechanistically plausible as the energetic cost of vertical displacement should scale with leg length. However, the small sample size (n=9) limits generalizability.

results.result: Eight of nine subjects showed significant correlations between straight path slope and chosen path tortuosity in per-path-segment analysis, though substantial variability exists. This suggests walkers use flexible learned heuristics rather than strict criteria for the slope-tortuosity trade-off.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 provides statistical support for the slope-tortuosity relationship at the individual path level. The interpretation (C60) regarding heuristics vs. strict criteria is reasonable given the observed variability, though alternative explanations (e.g., local terrain constraints) are not fully ruled out.

results.result: Walkers use vision to plan paths that account for terrain structure, selecting flatter routes that require planning ahead and changing direction to avoid height changes. This behavior reflects sensorimotor decision mechanisms integrating multiple factors including sensory information, motor constraints, costs, and path planning.
results.evaluation: These summary claims (C2-C6, C69-C73, C80-C84) are well-supported by the specific quantitative findings regarding path slope preferences, tortuosity-slope relationships, and CNN performance. The inference that planning is required (C72-C73) follows logically from the observed behavior, though the specific planning horizon is not directly measured in this study.

results.result: The terrain reconstruction and integration procedures provide greater precision than previous outdoor walking studies and enable novel analysis of how visual environment structure influences foothold selection. These methods should be generally useful for analyzing visually guided behavior in natural environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are supported by the demonstrated improvements over prior work (elimination of parallax and drift errors). Claim C63 accurately characterizes a gap in the field. Claim C81 regarding general utility is a reasonable inference given the successful application, though broader validation would strengthen this claim.

results.result: The preference for flatter paths is likely driven by energetic costs of vertical displacement, consistent with prior work showing humans converge to energetic optima on flat ground and can minimize costs on uneven terrain by modulating speed. Walkers may be adjusting behavior to minimize energetic costs in natural outdoor terrains.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 appropriately cite prior work on energetic optimization. However, claims C64 and C68 are speculative as no direct energetic measurements were made in this study. The inference is plausible and well-motivated, but remains unvalidated. Future work measuring actual energetic costs would be needed to confirm this interpretation.

results.result: The planning horizon in natural rocky terrain may differ from laboratory studies, with prior work suggesting 2 steps (lab), 5 steps (gaze in natural terrain), or 8-9 steps (biomechanical models). Differences may reflect terrain complexity, working memory load, or the role of peripheral vision.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 appropriately cite prior work on planning horizons. However, claims C78-C79 are speculative attempts to reconcile discrepancies between studies. The current study does not directly measure planning horizon, so these remain unresolved questions requiring future investigation with combined eye tracking and biomechanical modeling.

results.result: The dataset comprises 4,230 steps from 9 participants (347-603 steps each) walking over rocky terrain in Austin, TX and Berkeley, CA, recorded using mobile eye tracking (120 Hz eyes, 30 Hz scene) and motion capture (100 Hz, 17 IMUs) with synchronized timestamps.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C98 provide comprehensive methodological documentation of the dataset, equipment, and experimental procedures. The technical specifications are clearly stated and the synchronization approach (C93) is sound. The dataset size is adequate for the analyses performed, though relatively small for some statistical comparisons.

results.result: Gaze is clustered 2-3 steps ahead (from prior work), and off-path gaze points that precede turns may reflect how the visual system collects information for the trade-off between straight and flat paths.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 appropriately cites prior findings. Claim C101 describes an observation in the current data. However, claims C102-C103 regarding the functional role of off-path gaze are speculative. While the temporal pattern is suggestive, no quantitative analysis directly links off-path gaze to subsequent turning decisions. This remains a hypothesis for future testing.

results.result: Prior to this work, relatively little was known about vision-guided locomotion in natural environments. While gaze and body tracking technology is available, measurement of visual input in natural environments has been limited, and most locomotion research uses laboratory treadmill settings. Analysis of the relationship between visual environment structure and foothold/path selection has been missing.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C8, C10, C13, and C63 accurately characterize the state of the field and gaps in prior work. These statements are supported by the cited literature and provide appropriate context for the current study's contributions. The characterization is fair and well-documented.

results.result: Prior work has established that: visually guided walking involves complex sensorimotor decisions; humans converge to energetic optima and adopt preferred gaits; walkers use vision to find footholds in complex terrain; gaze patterns change with terrain demands; and deviations from preferred gait (including turns and vertical displacement) are energetically costly.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C11-C12, C14-C17, C32-C33, C35, C44, C65-C67 appropriately cite and characterize prior work that provides the foundation for the current study. The citations appear accurate and relevant. Claim C21 correctly identifies the data source. These claims provide essential context but are not novel findings of this work.

results.result: The terrain reconstruction method achieved median errors of 4.5 cm overall and 4.0 cm at foothold locations, with 95% quantiles of 20.0 cm and 16.8 cm respectively. These errors are below 20% of average foot length, indicating reasonably reliable 3D environment reconstructions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the technical achievement and methodological innovation. One reviewer stated the work is 'methodologically very impressive' and represents 'a further step forward towards understanding real-world locomotion.' Another noted the team 'managed to collect and analyze an unprecedented, one-of-a-kind dataset' and appreciated 'the numerous technical challenges.' The reconstruction reliability data were not questioned.

results.result: A CNN trained on retinocentric depth images predicted foothold locations above chance (median AUC > 0.5 for all subjects), demonstrating that depth information available to walkers is predictive of upcoming footholds and contributes to foothold finding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorsed this finding. One stated 'There is also good evidence for the third question, showing that retinocentric depth is predictive of chosen footholds' and described the analysis as having 'strong' results. Another reviewer noted 'they show using a neural network model that participants could choose the footholds based on their sensory (visual) information about depth.' The methodology and conclusions were accepted without critique.

results.result: Walkers prefer flatter paths: chosen path slopes (median 7.7-11.8°, mean 9.5°) were significantly lower than simulated random path slopes (median 9.1-19.2°, mean 14.9°), with simulated slopes being 5.56° larger on average (t(8)=7.64, p<<0.001).
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed significant concerns about this conclusion. One reviewer stated they were 'not entirely convinced by the evidence' and questioned whether the comparison between 'human tortuous paths taken and simulated straight-ahead paths never experienced by human' was valid. They noted 'it is not an apples-to-apples comparison' and preferred 'hard data than by unequal simulations.' Another reviewer was 'confused by aspects of the analysis' and found the simulations difficult to understand, particularly why flat steps 'were completely avoided' in Figure 8. The reviewer suggested the conclusion should be more cautiously stated as 'walkers changed direction more when straight-ahead paths seemed to have steeper height changes' rather than claiming intent to avoid.

results.result: Walkers choose indirect routes to avoid height changes: tortuosity (mean 1.09, median per subject 1.04-1.07) increased with straight path slope, suggesting walkers trade off path directness for flatness by changing direction to avoid steeper terrain.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly supported this finding. One stated 'I consider the evidence strongest for the first of the main questions' and noted 'The measure of straight-ahead steepness...is shown to be well correlated with tortuosity, effectively predicting when subjects will not walk straight ahead.' The editor noted this as a 'considerable strength,' specifically 'the ability to quantitatively predict when humans will walk more circuitously.' While one reviewer noted the finding 'is hardly surprising,' they acknowledged the systematic parametric investigation as the main contribution.

results.result: Subjects with shorter legs showed stronger correlations between straight path slope and tortuosity (r=-0.83, p=0.005), suggesting biomechanical scale effects where shorter individuals are more likely to choose longer, flatter paths when straight paths become steeper.
results.evaluation: A reviewer expressed substantial doubts about this finding, stating 'I had some misgivings about the fourth question' and 'I still have doubts' even after additional data were provided. They noted that 'Figure 18 provides more detail of the underlying data, with considerably lower correlations' and suspected 'Figure 10 benefits from some statistical artifacts due to binning and other operations.' The reviewer was 'rather suspicious of correlations of correlations' and questioned whether the dimensionless measures (tortuosity and slope) could truly demonstrate scale effects. They suggested 'simpler tests would better evidence' and concluded 'I feel that the evidence from this study is not that strong.'

results.result: Walkers plan ahead to select paths: they take terrain structure into account, plan individual foothold locations and flatter paths, demonstrating that locomotor behavior reflects sensorimotor decision mechanisms involving costs, sensory/motor information, and path planning.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the overall framework, one noted that 'some of the specific conclusions remain more suggestive at this point.' Another reviewer stated that 'from the data it is still not clear what actual visual features are used to choose among alternative routes or what the nature of the decision process is' and noted 'there is no way to express these ideas rigorously in such complex natural settings.' The evidence for planning was accepted as logical inference from the tortuosity findings, but the specific mechanisms remain unclear.

results.result: The terrain reconstruction and integration procedures using photogrammetry allowed greater precision than previous studies by eliminating errors from flat ground plane assumptions and IMU drift, enabling quantitative examination of how visual environment structure influences foothold selection.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously praised the methodological contribution. One stated 'The technical achievement is impressive' and 'I was impressed by the overarching outlook and ambitiousness of the team.' Another noted the authors 'have developed an impressive workflow to study gait and gaze in natural terrain' and the work is 'methodologically very impressive.' The editor emphasized this 'opens up new approaches to studying (visually guided) behavior in natural settings outside the lab.' The methodological innovation was consistently highlighted as a major strength.

comparisons.comparison: Strong agreement on CNN foothold prediction findings (C18, C30, C31). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED with high confidence. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate train-test splits and AUC metrics, while peer reviewers explicitly praised the 'strong' results and accepted methodology without critique.

Significant disagreement on leg length findings (C56, C57, C58). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED despite noting small sample size, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN with substantial doubts about statistical artifacts, correlations of correlations, and whether dimensionless measures can demonstrate scale effects.

Major disagreement on energetic cost interpretation (C19, C36-C43). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with strong quantitative evidence, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning the validity of comparing human tortuous paths to simulated straight paths as 'not an apples-to-apples comparison' and preferring more cautious conclusions.

Strong agreement on tortuosity-slope relationship (C20, C45-C49, C53-C55). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes comprehensive quantitative characterization with modest correlations, while peer reviewers consider this the 'strongest' evidence and a 'considerable strength' despite finding it 'hardly surprising.'

Strong agreement on methodological contributions (C61, C62, C81). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes improvements over prior work and reasonable inference about general utility, while peer reviewers unanimously praised the 'impressive' technical achievement and workflow as opening new approaches to studying natural behavior.

Partial disagreement on planning claims (C2, C4-C6, C72-C73, C80). OpenEval rates summary claims as SUPPORTED by quantitative findings, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting conclusions remain 'more suggestive' and that specific mechanisms and visual features used in decision processes remain unclear.

Strong agreement on reconstruction accuracy validation (C23-C26, C28). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative validation with appropriate context and sound methodology, while peer reviewers explicitly praised the 'methodologically very impressive' technical achievement without questioning the reconstruction reliability data.

Weak overlap on individual path analysis (C59). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED for slope-tortuosity relationship at individual path level, while peer reviewers' UNCERTAIN rating for R5 focuses on leg length correlations (C56-C58) with only tangential connection to C59.
